    10 Years of Minikube and the Future of Millions of Users

    Medya Ghazizadeh

    The speaker, who says he led minikube for seven years, looks back on the project's ten years, including its testing infrastructure, benchmarking tools, and growth in downloads. He describes the project's reduced staffing since 2025, his own burnout and departure from Google, and what he hopes the next maintainers will do.

    30 min slot · Level not listed · Session

    Community and open source adoptionPlatform engineering and developer experience

    Watch this if: you use minikube or maintain an open source project and want a longtime maintainer's account of how it was built and what it needs next.

    1. 5:04 The speaker says minikube lets users choose the container runtime and whether to run in a container or a VM, and that its VM drivers allow AI workloads on a MacBook's GPU.
    2. 14:42 The speaker says the project ended up with 300 integration tests across 21 environment combinations, and credits that testing with catching Kubernetes regressions.
    3. 19:21 The speaker says a benchmark showed minikube's slow start came from lacking a preload mechanism, not from the driver, and that with preloads a VM-driver cluster starts in 13 seconds.
    4. 22:05 The speaker says that in 2025 he absorbed the work of four or five people, and that he rejected advice to let the project break in order to attract funding.
    5. 24:33 The speaker says he can no longer work on minikube full-time and hopes the next maintainers grow the bench, end reliance on any single company, and gain representation in Kubernetes decision-making.

    10 Years, 10 Lessons

    Ram Iyengar

    Ram Iyengar of the Linux Foundation shares ten lessons from a decade around platform engineering, covering abstractions, definitions, metrics, costs, feedback and ownership. He argues that platform users are engineers who want to see inside the abstraction, and closes by saying developer experience is turning into agent experience.

    10 min slot · Any Level · Lightning Talk

    Platform engineering and developer experience

    Watch this if: you want an 11-minute list of one practitioner's platform lessons on abstractions, metrics, costs, feedback and ownership.

    1. 3:30 Iyengar says platform users are engineers who want to look inside an abstraction, and that handing one over to be used without examination creates friction with developer teams.
    2. 4:45 He says it is hard to agree on one definition of the platform, that it is more than a handful of tools put together, and that microservices got misread as letting every team pick any language.
    3. 7:01 On measurement, he asks whether time to first hello world or lead time for changes is the right metric, and whether 100% uptime counts as success if a database takes two days to get.
    4. 9:09 He calls feedback loops complaint boxes and suggests building a community instead: inner sourcing and growing platform advocates one team at a time.
    5. 10:15 He says developer experience has become agent experience, and closes with a bonus lesson 11: keep learning.

    1000 Clusters, 1 Smarter Brain: The Next Evolution of AIOps at Salesforce

    Anubhav Dhoot, Uttam Kumar

    The speakers say the accuracy of their incident troubleshooting agents fell as they added more data, and trace that to knowledge retrieval, evaluation, and agent design. They describe curated runbooks with hierarchical search, an LLM-as-judge pipeline calibrated with sampled on-call feedback, and a planner and critic design backed by a dependency knowledge graph, and report their own results.

    30 min slot · Any Level · Session

    Observability and reliabilityAI agents and automation

    Watch this if: you are building incident triage agents for a large Kubernetes fleet and want one team's account of why more data made theirs worse.

    1. 4:28 The speaker says accuracy dropped to 25% as more data was added, and names three bottlenecks: knowledge management, evaluation, and agent design.
    2. 6:17 The speaker describes a similarity trap where long Slack threads full of repeated error codes outranked the runbook holding the fix, even with a lower weight.
    3. 12:25 The speaker says they use Cochran's formula to ask on-call engineers for feedback on a sample, citing 88 samples per 1,000 transactions, and use it to calibrate the automated evals.
    4. 16:56 The speaker describes the new design: a planner agent forms several hypotheses from the knowledge graph, isolated sub-agents investigate them in parallel, and a critic agent validates the result.
    5. 22:02 The speaker reports a 60% improvement in time to troubleshoot, close to 900 hours saved, and 60 to 80% accuracy on their eval pipeline.

  • Lightning Talks

    5,000 Nodes in Minutes, Twice in a Week: A Pattern for Fleet-Wide Node Changes

    Alex Yuskauskas

    Alex Yuskauskas describes patching the Copy-Fail and Dirty Frag kernel CVEs across NVIDIA's fleet with NodeWright, a controller he maintains for changing node operating systems. His main point is to ship every node change together with a check that fails when the change did not work, declared as a Kubernetes resource so kubectl shows the rollout status.

    5 min slot · Advanced · Lightning Talk

    Accelerators and workload schedulingDelivery, GitOps and release safety

    Watch this if: you need to roll out a kernel or OS change to every node and prove it actually took effect.

    1. 0:18 Alex Yuskauskas recounts the Copy-Fail CVE workaround: a one-line modprobe drop-in file plus unloading the module with rmmod.
    2. 0:45 He explains the catch: if the module is in use, rmmod silently leaves it loaded, so nodes look fixed but are not until they reboot.
    3. 1:20 He says the NodeWright package ships the change and its check in the same image, and the check only passes once the module is gone from /proc/modules.
    4. 2:26 He describes rollout status as a fixed set of values (complete, in progress, erroring, blocked), which let the SRE team write an agent skill that stops and asks a human when a cluster does not complete.
    5. 3:05 He says they ran it across 16 clusters with thousands of nodes in half an hour, then folded Dirty Frag into the same package so the next CVE is a YAML change.

    Agentic Ops: Building Guardrails for Autonomous AI with Policy-as-Code

    Pavan Madduri

    The speaker describes the guardrails he wants before agents act on production clusters: GitOps-only writes, a shadow mode, least privilege and Kyverno policies as a deterministic ring around the agent. He frames unsafe agent actions as a permissions problem, not a model problem, and sorts actions into ones the agent may take alone, ones that need human approval and ones that are always denied.

    25 min slot · Level not listed · Session

    Security, identity and policyAI agents and automation

    Watch this if: You are considering letting AI agents remediate incidents on Kubernetes and want a staged, policy-backed way to limit what they can do.

    1. 0:56 The speaker describes an agent that, when a restart did not clear an alert, scaled the workload down and deleted its PVC, causing a data recovery incident.
    2. 3:21 He lays out autonomy levels from L0, where humans do everything, through suggestions and shadow mode to L3 with guardrails, and says he would not suggest L4 full autonomy without concrete guardrails.
    3. 4:56 He sets the rule that the agent only writes to Git, so every fix becomes a pull request that a human approves and a policy check validates before it reaches the cluster.
    4. 12:20 He shows a hard-deny Kyverno policy that matches every service account in the agent namespace and blocks actions on PVCs, namespaces, StatefulSets, roles and role bindings.
    5. 14:00 He sorts actions into three colors: green ones such as restarts and bounded scaling the agent does alone, amber ones that need human approval, and red ones such as data deletion that are always denied.

    AI on Kubernetes Is Just a Pod With a GPU (and That's the Problem)

    Graziano Casto

    Graziano Casto compares deploying a web application with deploying a model on Kubernetes, starting from a plain Deployment that runs a vLLM container. He names three differences, which are whole-number GPU allocation, slow startup while model weights load, and requests that cost very different amounts of GPU work, and for each he points to projects he says address it.

    12 min slot · Level not listed · Session

    AI inference and servingAccelerators and workload scheduling

    Watch this if: You run web applications on Kubernetes and want a short orientation on what changes with model serving before choosing AI talks to watch.

    1. 0:36 The speaker shows what he calls the easiest way to deploy a model on Kubernetes: an ordinary Deployment running a vLLM container that serves a Llama 3.1 model.
    2. 3:01 He says a GPU is requested as a whole number, so a model that does not use a full GPU still leaves it overprovisioned.
    3. 3:43 He lists dynamic resource allocation in Kubernetes, HAMi for software-level enforcement and NVIDIA MIG for hardware partitioning as ways to share a GPU.

    5. 6:57 He says round-robin load balancing does not fit chat workloads, and describes llm-d's KV-cache-aware routing, built on the Gateway API Inference Extension, as sending a conversation back to where its context lives.

    Allocating Kubernetes Idle Per-Instance — Letting Scale Do What Fairness Rules Couldn't

    Vinicius Krischke

    Vinicius Krischke describes how Nubank allocates Kubernetes idle cost node by node instead of spreading it across all workloads by their share of requests. He argues that this sends a cost signal to the services that cause idle, and that at large scale the allocation evens out without hand-written fairness rules.

    5 min slot · Advanced · Lightning Talk

    Accelerators and workload scheduling

    Watch this if: you allocate Kubernetes costs to teams and want idle cost to reach the services that cause it.

    1. 0:19 Vinicius Krischke describes the common approach: take the whole month's idle and spread it across services by their share of requests.
    2. 0:57 He explains Nubank's alternative: allocate idle per node, to the pods running on that node.
    3. 1:35 He says this shifts idle cost to the services that generate it and sends a cost signal, while engineers still decide whether a resource is worth it.
    4. 2:31 He takes the fairness objection, a service landing on a node next to a wasteful one, and argues the odds of that repeating are small.
    5. 3:04 He says that as the number of instances grows the allocation approaches the mean, so no complicated rules are needed.

    Anatomy of an Outage: When Bursty ML Workloads Break the Kubernetes Scheduler

    Cellan Hall, Jenny Vega, Karol Szuster

    Two engineers from Isomorphic Labs and a Kueue maintainer from Google recount a 10-day outage in which autoscaled inference deployments flooded a cluster with pending Kueue workloads. They walk through its three phases and causes, the upstream fixes in Kueue and Kubernetes, and the cluster, alerting and autoscaling changes they say they made afterward.

    30 min slot · Advanced · Session

    Accelerators and workload schedulingObservability and reliabilityKubernetes internals and runtimes

    Watch this if: You run autoscaled batch or inference workloads through Kueue and want to see how pending objects can take down scheduling.

    1. 6:35 Jenny Vega says a flood of pending pods and workloads in February 2026 pushed a production cluster into a 10-day outage in three phases, ending with 20 hours of no scheduling.
    2. 8:14 Karol Szuster says the Kueue controller restarts came from one shared client-side rate-limit bucket that also covered leader election, so a storm of reconciles stopped the lease from being renewed.
    3. 9:52 Jenny Vega shows how unschedulable GPU replicas at the head of a shared queue kept admissible CPU work from being reached, and says the team split the queue while Kueue added scheduling equivalence hashing upstream.
    4. 14:38 The speakers explain that after a restart the API server had to call Kueue's conversion webhook for every workload to rebuild its watch cache, which could not finish within the five-minute compaction interval.
    5. 21:06 Cellan Hall says the team now feeds the admitted pod count back into the KEDA scaling trigger, and reports 80 percent fewer pending Kueue workloads and 40 percent fewer workload objects in etcd.

He walks through the design choices he says keep the scheduling loop fast on very large clusters, then discusses soft slicing, defragmentation and the lack of transactional binding in the API server.

    30 min slot · Advanced · Session

    Accelerators and workload schedulingKubernetes internals and runtimesNetworking and connectivity

    1. 1:27 Dai frames the problem as gang scheduling plus topology-aware scheduling and describes two gang modes: a full gang where every pod must run, and replicas that are each a gang but fail independently.
    2. 6:47 He says the team models every cluster as a tree of network domains whose leaves are TPU slices, Trainium servers or GPU nodes, and built a drop-in replacement scheduler that jobs select by scheduler name.
    3. 8:15 He describes the control loop: take a snapshot of the cluster, plan all pending jobs from highest to lowest priority, and schedule jobs rather than pods, with the loop kept within 10 seconds on their largest cluster.
    4. 16:48 He says scoring nodes only once for jobs that are identical from a scheduling perspective is by far the largest scaling factor in their system.
    5. 23:55 As something that does not work well, Dai points to gang binding without transactions in the API server: some of the bind calls can fail, forcing eviction of the pods already bound.

    1. 2:36 Rita Zhang gives the motivating case for conditional authorization: a controller that may update a pod but should only touch its own finalizer currently needs one access rule split across authorization and admission, which must be kept aligned.
    2. 9:25 David Eads describes the new conditional authorizer interface, in which an authorizer that answers maybe stores its conditions in the request context so admission can evaluate them once the object is available, and results are downgraded if the admission plugin is turned off.

    Sharik Pahwa, Hardeep Singh Tiwana

    Sharik Pahwa and Hardeep Singh Tiwana demonstrate a healthy cluster going read-only after a storm of status patches fills a deliberately small etcd quota, and then trace the triggers and the failure back through etcd's multi-version storage. They walk through recovery with compaction and defragmentation and suggest alerts, admission policies and scheduled defragmentation to prevent a repeat.

    30 min slot · Advanced · Session

    Observability and reliabilityKubernetes internals and runtimes

    Watch this if: you run Kubernetes control planes or write controllers and want to understand how frequent status and annotation writes can fill etcd, and how to recover and guard against it.

    1. 3:22 In the demo, Pahwa says a script creates 80 pod replicas and sends a storm of status patches, each of which makes etcd store a full copy of the object, until the cluster with a 100 MB etcd quota turns read-only while the pods keep running.
    2. 4:43 Pahwa lists triggers that he says compound: scheduler retries on unschedulable pods, crash-looping containers, node lease renewals, controllers that write status without a change, annotations used as a message channel, and jobs without TTLs.
    3. 10:19 He argues that a read-only cluster is worse than an outage because pod status still shows Running and alarms stay green, and failures then arrive as a cascade of alarms that hides the etcd cause.
    4. 18:03 Tiwana explains that compaction only marks old revisions as deleted and leaves the file size unchanged, so space comes back only after defragmentation, which he advises running on one etcd member at a time because it pauses that member.
    5. 24:04 As a preventive guardrail, Tiwana shows a validating admission policy that limits how large an annotation or status update can be, and a test in which the oversized write is rejected.

    Five Stages of Kubernetes Security Grief

    Ann Wallace, Kavitha Daula

    Ann Wallace and Kavitha Daula walk through denial, anger, bargaining, depression and acceptance as stages of Kubernetes security, with Wallace voicing what teams say at each stage and Daula describing a CVE in the shared Linux kernel or container runtime that she says undercuts it. They conclude that namespaces and policies remain needed but do not give a workload its own kernel, and argue for hypervisor-based isolation with a guest kernel per workload.

    1. 3:09 For the denial stage, Daula says Kubernetes namespaces organize workloads but containers still share one Linux kernel, and walks through CVE-2022-0492, where a container could use the cgroups v1 release agent to run code as root on the host.
    2. 5:44 For anger, she describes a Netfilter use-after-free reachable from a container's own user and network namespaces, which she says researchers exploited to become root even though the application never touches firewall rules.
    3. 8:42 For bargaining, she recounts the 2019 runc escape in which the host runc binary could be overwritten, noting that running as non-root or enforcing SELinux could have prevented it but that policy does not patch a vulnerable runtime.
    4. 11:36 For depression, she explains Leaky Vessels, where a leaked file descriptor in runc gave a container access to the host file system, and says it covered four CVEs across runc and BuildKit.
    5. 13:46 For acceptance, Daula argues for changing the isolation boundary itself by giving each workload its own guest kernel behind a hypervisor, and says vulnerabilities do not disappear and the security policies are still needed.

    Green Dashboards, Broken Clusters: Taming Stale Watches in Kubernetes Operators

    Michael Aspinwall, Alvaro Aleman

    Michael Aspinwall and Alvaro Aleman explain how a controller that reads from a lagging informer cache can miss its own writes, using a DaemonSet controller case in which duplicate pods were created on every node. They describe the upstream Kubernetes work on comparable resource versions, informer staleness metrics and a consistency store in client-go, and the different approach controller-runtime takes with a client that waits for the cache to catch up.

    30 min slot · Advanced · Session

    Observability and reliabilityKubernetes internals and runtimes

    Watch this if: you write or operate Kubernetes controllers and want to know how stale informer caches cause duplicate or wrong actions, and what client-go and controller-runtime now offer to avoid them.

    1. 3:47 Aspinwall walks through the case study: the DaemonSet controller's write expectations expire after about five minutes, so when the pod informer lags longer than that, the controller sees no pod in its stale cache and creates another one on the same node.
    2. 5:53 He says KEP-5504 extends to clients the guarantee that resource versions can be compared, so a controller can tell from the version returned by its write whether its cache has caught up.
    3. 6:21 He describes a new metric on every informer store in client-go that can be subtracted from the API server's watch cache resource version, and shows a scale-test graph in which one API server falls up to 350,000 resource versions behind.
    4. 7:17 He explains the consistency store, which records the resource version of each write and returns an error at the start of the next reconcile until the store has synced past it, and says it is already in the DaemonSet, Job, StatefulSet and ReplicaSet controllers.
    5. 18:27 Aleman describes controller-runtime's consistent client as two layers: reads that start after a write block until the write finishes, and then wait until the cache has reached the resource version that write returned.

    Kubernetes Secrets Were a Bad Idea. Now What?

    Maxime Coquerel

    Maxime Coquerel argues, as his own opinion, that Kubernetes Secrets are risky because they are only base64 encoded in etcd, readable with broad RBAC permissions and have no lifecycle. He recommends encrypting etcd with a customer managed key, keeping secrets out of Git and mounting secrets from a real vault at runtime with the Secrets Store CSI Driver or the OpenBao agent.

    5 min slot · Beginner · Lightning Talk

    Security, identity and policy

    Watch this if: you are deciding whether Kubernetes Secrets are good enough for your platform or which alternative to use.

    1. 0:43 Maxime Coquerel says a Kubernetes Secret is stored in etcd only base64 encoded, not encrypted, and that etcd is a key value store, not a vault.
    2. 1:46 He lists the weaknesses he sees, including that anyone with get, list or watch permissions can read secret contents.
    3. 2:05 He adds that Kubernetes Secrets have no lifecycle: no expiration date and no automatic renewal.
    4. 2:47 His first recommendation is to encrypt etcd with a customer managed key, which he says managed services such as Azure Kubernetes Service support.
    5. 3:49 He compares Sealed Secrets, SOPS and External Secrets Operator, and recommends mounting secrets as files at runtime with the Secrets Store CSI Driver or the OpenBao agent.

    Kubernetes Solutions for Agent-Shaped Problems

    Tim Hockin, Dmitry Berkovich

    Tim Hockin and Dmitry Berkovich of Google say agent workloads are bursty, run untrusted code and have a human waiting, which makes one sandboxed pod per agent session wasteful and slow on Kubernetes. They present Agent Substrate, an open source system built on Kubernetes that suspends idle agents to snapshots and resumes them on request, and spend the second half answering audience questions about policy, autoscaling, memory and where it fits.

    30 min slot · Any Level · Session

    AI agents and automationKubernetes internals and runtimes

    Watch this if: you run or plan to run many agent sessions on your own Kubernetes clusters and want the reasoning behind Agent Substrate from its authors, plus a long Q&A on its current limits.

    1. 0:47 Hockin and Berkovich name three traits of agent workloads: they are bursty and mostly idle, they run untrusted code that must be sandboxed, and a human is usually waiting for the response.
    2. 6:57 Hockin states the three design principles of Agent Substrate (security by default, near-zero cost for idle agents, fast wake-up) and what he calls aspirational goals: billions of agents per cluster, 10,000 activations per second and wake-up in about 100 milliseconds.
    3. 9:16 Berkovich defines the five terms: an actor runs one agent session, an actor template configures it, a worker is the pod that hosts actors, a node-level manager handles images and snapshots, and a network layer routes requests in and applies policy to traffic out.
    4. 13:06 He explains resume speed through layers: volumes always survive, while root filesystem changes and the memory snapshot are reused only if the OCI image is unchanged, otherwise the actor cold starts from its volumes.
    5. 15:26 Hockin describes a use case they see often: a managed agent service runs the agentic loop while the work it triggers runs in Agent Substrate inside the customer's own cluster, where it can be audited and shut off.

    Linkerd, The Service Mesh for Everyone: gRPC Load Balancing & More

    Joe Fuller

    Joe Fuller of Buoyant explains why gRPC over a single HTTP/2 connection defeats connection-level load balancing on Kubernetes and presents a benchmark he says Buoyant ran comparing Linkerd with Istio and Cilium. He then covers what Linkerd 2.20 adds, mainly rate-limit-aware load balancing and a new circuit breaking mode, both alpha and opt-in, and what has shipped in edge releases for 2.21.

    30 min slot · Level not listed · Session

    Networking and connectivity

    Watch this if: you run gRPC services on Kubernetes and want to understand per-request load balancing, or you are deciding whether to turn on the new Linkerd 2.20 overload features.

    1. 4:21 Joe Fuller explains the gRPC problem: a client opens one HTTP/2 connection, every request lands on one pod, and scaling up does not help because new pods get none of the existing connections.
    2. 6:58 He describes a benchmark he says Buoyant's engineers ran on EKS against Istio in ambient and sidecar mode and Cilium in L7 mode, and reports Linkerd at about 92% of no-mesh throughput.
    3. 10:51 He describes the failure mode 2.20 targets: an overloaded pod that rejects requests quickly with 429 or RESOURCE_EXHAUSTED looks like the fastest endpoint to a latency-based balancer and gets more traffic.
    4. 12:11 He explains rate-limit-aware load balancing: the client proxy records a penalty of five seconds by default, or the server's back-off hint, instead of the fast rejection, so traffic shifts away and then returns as the penalty decays.
    5. 20:06 He says the destination controller no longer keeps a per-subscriber endpoint snapshot, which he says cut control plane memory by about 84% in load tests, and that native sidecars are GA and on by default.

    Not All Memory Is Equal: How To Properly Observe Memory Usage

    Braydon Kains, Roger Coll

    The speakers explain why host, node, pod and process memory metrics differ, tracing each to the Linux file it is read from and to how the kernel treats anonymous and file-backed pages. Using the OpenTelemetry Collector contrib binary in live demos, they show that much of its resident memory is file-backed data that can be reclaimed, and they recommend collecting system usage, container usage and working set together.

    30 min slot · Advanced · Session

    Observability and reliabilityKubernetes internals and runtimes

    Watch this if: You size memory limits or alert on memory in Kubernetes and want to know what RSS, usage and working set each count.

    1. 4:40 Roger Coll says the metrics differ because they are read from different files: system memory usage comes from /proc/meminfo, while the kubelet's node usage, RSS and working set come from the cgroup memory stats.
    2. 11:17 Braydon Kains says an OOM kill happens when there are no clean file-backed pages left to reclaim, not simply when a process is over its limit.
    3. 15:34 Roger Coll says the Collector contrib binary has 12,000 Go init functions, about 17 megabytes loaded into RAM, which run once at startup.
    4. 17:41 In a live demo, forcing a reclaim removes a large share of the contrib Collector's memory and much of it never pages back in; Braydon Kains adds that working set drops only after a reclaim classifies file pages as inactive.
    5. 23:14 Roger Coll says working set is the value Kubernetes treats as memory usage and the one the kubelet uses to pick pods to evict under node memory pressure.

  • Operations + Performance

    Surviving the Churn: Read Replicas and Controllers for Busy Kubernetes Clusters

    Ryan Brewster

    The speaker, who works at Anthropic, argues that large Kubernetes clusters stay stable only while every component stays on its watch stream, and that falling off it under churn can set off failures that load tests do not show. He explains where lock contention in controllers and the API server causes this, and describes structural isolation measures such as lock-free snapshots in controllers and caching read proxies in front of the API server.

    30 min slot · Advanced · Session

    Observability and reliabilityKubernetes internals and runtimes

    Watch this if: You operate large, high-churn Kubernetes clusters and want to understand why watch streams and lock contention decide whether the control plane survives a bad minute.

    1. 3:14 The speaker gives an example of metastability: a list of pods on a node is served from the API server's watch cache until the cache falls more than three seconds behind, then falls through to the storage layer and can knock it over.
    2. 12:04 He explains that any controller in the kube-controller-manager holding an informer read lock too long stalls event processing, so controllers act on stale state, and some then create duplicate pods and add more churn.
    3. 15:17 The speaker proposes copy-on-write snapshots in controllers so readers never take a lock, and says the roughly 10x slower data structure is worth it because synchronization, not map speed, is the bottleneck.
    4. 20:59 He describes putting caching proxies in front of the API servers to take heavy reads off them, at the cost of a few milliseconds of delay and another distributed component to operate.
    5. 27:00 The speaker says a slow watch client should be allowed to stall and catch up from the watch cache's shared history instead of being kicked off, and points to a Kubernetes enhancement proposal he hopes lands in 1.38.

    Two-Stage OTel Aggregation: Taming Istio Cardinality at 10k-Pod Scale

    Evelyn (Chungyu) Chen

    The speaker, from Yahoo, describes cutting the Istio metric series of a large production cluster by 86% by aggregating away pod-level identity in OpenTelemetry Collectors, first on each node and then at a gateway. She walks through the processor order this needs and the problems her team says it hit along the way, including counters that went down after pod restarts and data lost at one backend.

    30 min slot · Advanced · Session

    Observability and reliabilityNetworking and connectivity

    Watch this if: You run Istio at scale, pay per metric series, and want to see how one team aggregated pod-level labels away inside the OpenTelemetry Collector.

    1. 0:26 The speaker says one production cluster with over 800 nodes and 24,000 pods went from more than 2 million active series to an 86% smaller set, which she puts at about $140,000 a year saved on that cluster.
    2. 8:05 She explains the per-node steps: the transform processor deletes pod and container identifiers at the resource level, a batch step lets data points meet, groupbyattrs promotes the app label to the resource, and metricstransform sums the series.
    3. 12:47 She explains why the pipeline runs twice: each node agent collapses its own pods' metrics, then the gateway removes node identity and aggregates across nodes to one series per app.
    4. 15:05 She says summing cumulative counters across pods made totals drop when a pod restarted, producing rate spikes, and that the fix was converting to delta with cumulativetodelta first and rewriting queries from rate to sum_over_time.
    5. 21:16 She says a second vendor's backend stored only one point per second per series, so values pushed by three gateway pods in the same second collided and only the last was kept, a problem she says is still open.

    Akhil Mohan

    Akhil Mohan of VMware by Broadcom, a containerd maintainer, retraces how a CSI pod on an internal cluster sat in CreateContainerError for 19 hours after a hypervisor power failure while its containers were in fact running. He traces it to a VM that booted about eight minutes in the future, so tokens were issued in the future and kubelet's sorting of containers by creation time got stuck once chrony stepped the clock back, and he describes the fix of starting kubelet only after time sync.

    30 min slot · Any Level · Session

    Observability and reliabilityKubernetes internals and runtimes

    Watch this if: you operate Kubernetes nodes on virtual machines and want a worked example of debugging from a stuck pod down to the hardware clock.

    1. 0:26 Mohan lays out the symptom: a CSI pod in CreateContainerError with over 5,000 retries failing on a container name reservation, while crictl on the node shows the same containers already running.
    2. 8:51 He finds kube-proxy rejected by the API server because its service account token is not valid yet, issued by a control plane VM whose clock was ahead of the other two.
    3. 10:08 Journal logs show the time jumping backwards 45 seconds after boot: he says the VM inherited a clock about eight minutes ahead from the ESXi host and chrony stepped it back in one go, after kubelet had already started.
    4. 18:55 He explains the loop: kubelet sorts container statuses by created-at wall clock time, so the attempt created on the future clock always looks newest and kubelet keeps trying to recreate an attempt that is already running.
    5. 21:36 The fix he describes is ordering the kubelet systemd unit after a chrony wait service with a 180 second timeout, chosen so a node boots slower instead of never booting when NTP is unavailable.

    4. 5:21 Michael Bolot says they replaced a vendor-provided egress proxy, which he calls expensive, with an Envoy-based explicit proxy that serves workloads in both environments.
    5. 6:55 They describe an xDS configuration server that gives each proxy least-access configuration based on its identity, fed by a simplified REST API so users do not write Envoy or Istio resources.

    Emily Chen of Akuity and Flux maintainer Leigh Capili compare the design priorities of Argo CD and Flux and describe ways teams run both, such as Flux for cluster add-ons across a fleet and Argo CD for developer applications. In live demos, Flux bootstraps Argo CD, a Flux signature failure shows up as a degraded Argo CD application, and Kargo promotes a Flux Helm release of cert-manager across three virtual clusters.

    2. 10:12 The speakers describe a common split where Flux handles fleet management and cluster add-ons while Argo CD serves application developers.
    3. 16:34 In the demo, Capili pushes an unsigned chart and the signature verification failure from Flux appears in the Argo CD interface.
    4. 20:19 Chen's Kargo promotion of cert-manager commits directly to Git for Flux to pick up, without using Argo CD.
    5. 22:16 Capili says Kargo has only one health checker, for Argo CD applications, and proposes one that reads kstatus so Kargo could understand Flux and other tools.

    Your Agent Needs a Platform: Cloud Native Infrastructure for Multi-Agent AI Systems

    Soham Ghadge

    Soham Ghadge describes problems he met running AI agents in production, such as crashes midway through a task, rate limits, repeated model calls and poor visibility, and maps each one to existing cloud native tools. He proposes defining agents as Kubernetes custom resources, saving each model call as a Dapr workflow step, queueing tasks through NATS JetStream and tracing with OpenTelemetry.

    30 min slot · Advanced · Session

    AI agents and automationPlatform engineering and developer experience

    Watch this if: you are building multi-agent systems and want a short overview of which cloud native tools cover crash recovery, queueing and tracing.

    1. 2:35 Ghadge lists his mapping of agent problems to tools, starting with describing each agent as a Kubernetes object through a CRD.
    2. 3:38 Ghadge shows a simplified agent definition as a Kubernetes object, with replicas, maximum tasks per copy and what the agent reads from and writes to.
    3. 7:00 Ghadge says to put every AI model call inside a saved step so that after a restart Dapr reuses the saved answer instead of paying for the call again.
    4. 7:39 Ghadge describes an agent queue, which he compares to a Redis queue, so agents do not handle every request directly.
    5. 9:48 Ghadge's conclusion is to treat an agentic system like a distributed system and agents like microservices.

    Your CI's Mistaken Identity

    Andrew McNamara, Maia Iyer

    Andrew McNamara and Maia Iyer say a namespace and service account can tell you where a CI task runs without telling you what it should be allowed to do. They describe pairing per-task workload identities with admission-time policy and using those identities to authorize access and sign attestations.

    30 min slot · Any Level · Session

    Delivery, GitOps and release safetySecurity, identity and policy

    Watch this if: You want to avoid giving every task in a Kubernetes CI pipeline the same privileges.

    1. 4:30 The speakers explain that SPIRE can use more than namespace and service account when assigning workload identities, so CI pods in the same namespace can have different roles.
    2. 9:19 The speakers explain that a Tekton bundle's digest changes when its task definition changes, and show where Sigstore signatures and attestations can be stored.
    3. 14:14 The speakers describe using Kyverno admission policy to require extra verification before a task can get a production identity.
    4. 16:57 In the live demo, the speakers show that an unsigned task from an untrusted catalog was blocked before a pod was scheduled.
    5. 22:21 The speakers explain how task-scoped identities let a verification policy check not just for an attestation, but for the specific CI task expected to produce it.

    Your GPU Nodes Deserve Better: Flatcar Container Linux for AI Workloads

    Jan Bronicki, Sayan Chowdhury

    Flatcar maintainers Jan Bronicki and Sayan Chowdhury introduce Flatcar Container Linux as an immutable, image-based operating system provisioned from a Butane configuration, and explain its read-only /usr partition, A/B updates and release channels. In recorded demos they provision a VM, add Kubernetes as a systemd system extension, bring up GPU nodes with NVIDIA drivers shipped as an extension, and switch driver versions with a config change and a reboot.

    30 min slot · Level not listed · Session

    Kubernetes internals and runtimesAccelerators and workload scheduling

    Watch this if: you run GPU nodes on Kubernetes and want to see how an immutable host OS handles NVIDIA driver updates and rollbacks.

    1. 5:12 Jan Bronicki presents the idea of the operating system as code: Flatcar is provisioned rather than installed, from one Butane YAML file applied at first boot, and the whole OS updates atomically so machines do not drift.
    2. 12:02 Sayan Chowdhury explains A/B partition updates, in which a new version is staged to the inactive /usr partition and becomes active after a successful boot, with automatic rollback to the previous version if the boot fails.
    3. 18:42 In a recorded demo, Jan Bronicki adds Kubernetes to a Flatcar VM as a systemd system extension declared in Butane, and shows kubeadm and kubectl available under the read-only /usr.
    4. 22:18 He explains that NVIDIA drivers are packaged as a system extension pinned to the kernel and Flatcar release, so they update and roll back with the OS, then shows nvidia-smi working on a Flatcar GPU node.
    5. 26:22 Sayan Chowdhury shows a recorded driver change on an AWS instance, editing the extension configuration from the 570 driver to 580 and rebooting to load the newer driver.

    Your Peers Are Struggling With LLM Inference on Kubernetes Too. Here's What the Data Says.

    Danielle Cook, Andy Suderman

    Danielle Cook of Akamai and Andy Suderman of Fairwinds walk through an Akamai-commissioned survey of 200 practitioners running AI in production, along with CNCF, Forrester and Cast AI figures, to show where teams say inference on Kubernetes is hard. They group the problems into scheduling, scaling, routing, placement and ownership, and close with five steps they recommend, from starting on an AI-conformant cluster to setting a time-to-first-token SLO.

    30 min slot · Any Level · Session

    AI inference and servingObservability and reliability

    Watch this if: you run LLM inference on Kubernetes and want survey numbers to compare your latency targets, GPU utilization and routing setup against.

    1. 4:33 Cook presents the survey's performance expectations: 82% of respondents need an end-to-end response within 500 milliseconds, 64% within 250, and nearly half expect to roll back within 15 minutes when inference degrades.
    2. 8:19 Suderman cites a Cast AI figure of 5% average GPU utilization across Kubernetes clusters and suggests Dynamic Resource Allocation, Kueue and right-sized requests as practical responses.
    3. 10:48 Suderman argues against autoscaling inference on CPU and recommends scaling on latency signals such as time to first token, using the metrics vLLM exposes with KEDA.
    4. 12:01 Cook explains why round-robin load balancing fits LLM replicas poorly, since each has its own KV cache, and relays an example where an inference-aware gateway doubled prefix cache hits from 35% to 70%.
    5. 22:15 The speakers give their five steps: start from an AI-conformant cluster, cut model startup time, autoscale on inference signals, put an inference-aware gateway in front, and set a p95 time-to-first-token SLO.

  • AI Inference + Agentic

    Zero-Gap GPU Execution: Building Secure, Pre-Warmed Pod Runtimes for High-Velocity AI Agents

    Ankit Goyal, Cong Gu

    The LinkedIn speakers present Firepool, their control plane that hands GPU jobs from agents and reinforcement learning loops to pools of already running pods, so no pod is created on the job's critical path. They describe how pods are reset and reused per caller, how standby pods parked on busy GPUs with HAMi and Volcano take over when a job ends, and report that 19 of 20 pod requests in production are served from warm pods.

    30 min slot · Any Level · Session

    Accelerators and workload schedulingAI agents and automationKubernetes internals and runtimes

    Watch this if: You run agent or reinforcement learning loops that need GPUs in short repeated bursts and want to cut pod cold starts without keeping GPUs idle.

    1. 5:07 Ankit Goyal says that with the image cached a new GPU pod takes 20 to 30 seconds to start, and that an agent running hundreds of GPU experiments pays that cost each time when it lives on CPU nodes.
    2. 8:48 He walks through a job submission and says there is no pod creation in the critical path: the dispatcher claims a warm pod and the Firepool agent inside it fetches the job's code and runs it.
    3. 14:24 Cong Gu describes the reuse rules: the Firepool agent kills the job's process tree and verifies the reset or deletes the pod, and an idle pod is held only for the caller that used it.
    4. 19:06 Ankit Goyal explains zero-gap: they use HAMi and Volcano only to schedule several pods onto one GPU, where one pod runs a job with the whole card and the rest are standby pods ready to take over.
    5. 22:09 He says Firepool pods run sandboxed with no egress by default, and outbound calls go through a sidecar proxy that injects credentials and checks policy, so agents never hold real credentials.

    Joe Nathan Abellard and Li Zhuyu describe how Bloomberg runs Karmada as a managed, highly available multi-cluster orchestration layer across data centers. They cover the operator, observability, scale testing with KWOK and ClusterLoader2, and the scheduler changes they made for large fan-out workloads.

    25 min slot · Intermediate · Session

    Observability and reliabilityPlatform engineering and developer experience

    Watch this if: you run or plan a multi-cluster Kubernetes platform and want a detailed Karmada case study covering HA, observability and scheduler tuning.

    1. 2:11 The speakers say data center redundancy is a Bloomberg-wide mandate and that they chose Karmada, which has a standard kube API server, its own scheduler and placement driven by propagation policies.
    2. 8:06 They describe a managed Karmada operator they built that gives each tenant its own namespace and control planes, sets up ingress and registers member clusters automatically from a cluster inventory API.
    3. 10:14 They walk through an HA topology where every control plane runs on host clusters in several data centers, sharing a DNS endpoint and an etcd cluster spread over three data centers, and go through which failures it survives.
    4. 19:48 For scale tests they say they use KWOK so only one of each cluster's 1,000 nodes is real, drive load with ClusterLoader2 and measure end-to-end propagation latency with a sidecar controller.
    5. 29:43 They report that a separate fan-out scheduler for duplicated workloads cut P99 propagation latency from over three minutes at 20 objects per second to under one second at 50 objects per second in their tests.

    Zero-Trust Telemetry: Stopping AI-Powered Poisoning Attacks on Observability Pipelines

    Chad M. Crowell, Diana Todea

    Chad M. Crowell and Diana Todea describe why telemetry should be treated as untrusted input when it feeds automated decisions. They propose independent controls for transport, query access, and network policy, then discuss how to verify those controls in Kubernetes.

    30 min slot · Advanced · Session

    Observability and reliabilitySecurity, identity and policy

    Watch this if: telemetry drives automated responses and you want to limit what each source and consumer can do.

    1. 13:37 The speakers describe using mutual TLS between OpenTelemetry Collectors and backends, and explain that verifying the sender does not verify that the data is true.
    2. 16:43 They propose checking the identity and scope of human and agent queries with fine-grained role-based access, then logging those decisions for audit.
    3. 20:02 They recommend default-deny network policies for the telemetry namespace, with explicit allowances for the application-to-collector and collector-to-backend flows.
    4. 22:42 They describe using Falco with Kubernetes audit events to detect suspicious activity, complementing the communication limits from network policy.
    5. 23:54 They recommend validating which sources feed Prometheus federation and restricting who can reach federation endpoints and exporters.

  • Platform Engineering Day

    “Allowed but Unsupported”: When Platform Support Boundaries Meet Enterprise Reality

    Niranjan Shankar

    Niranjan Shankar describes how the Azure Kubernetes Service team opened limited escape hatches for enterprise customers and what happened when support ownership was unclear. He uses packet loss at the boundary between a self-managed network plugin and a managed service mesh to show why teams need to name who owns the risk.

    25 min slot · Any Level · Session

    Platform engineering and developer experienceSecurity, identity and policy

    Watch this if: You need to give advanced platform users more control without leaving production support ownership ambiguous.

    1. 4:38 Shankar introduces the 'Allowed but Unsupported' tier and uses Istio to show how a team can allow a few EnvoyFilter uses, support routine MeshConfig fields, and block higher-risk settings.
    2. 11:39 He uses packet loss with a self-managed CNI and a provider-managed service mesh to explain why the boundary between supported and unsupported parts is hard to diagnose during an incident.
    3. 13:12 He recalls customers having trouble migrating from self-managed Prometheus to the managed offering because it did not support a rule resource they used.
    4. 20:35 He recommends giving unsupported features a signpost: a way to get best-effort help, an internal owner for production risk, and a path back to a supported option.
    5. 23:08 He closes with criteria for deciding what to expose, including whether teams can isolate the security risk, find an owner, or offer a narrower subset instead of the entire API.
